newsitem.title: ITALY: Stet shareholders approve Telecom Italia merger.
newsitem.headline: Stet shareholders approve Telecom Italia merger.

text.p: Shareholders of Italian state telecommunications holding Stet approved on Wednesday a merger with operating company Telecom Italia, easing the way towards privatising the merged entity.

Stet chairman Guido Rossi declared that a motion in favour of the merger had been approved at the end of an extraordinary shareholders' meeting at the company's headquarters in the northwestern city of Turin.

Earlier on Wednesday shareholders of Telecom Italia, the world's sixth largest telecommunications operator by number of subscribers, also voted in favour of the link-up, which aims to create a single national champion in the industry.

The merger is an important preparatory step ahead of the group's planned privatisation, which the government wants to complete before the end of the year, pending approval by parliament of an agency to regulate the industry.
"The problem now is to pull off the privatisation," Rossi told shareholders at the end of the meeting.

Newspapers have reported that Rossi, a company lawyer brought in after Stet's former top management was ousted by the government earlier this year, was weighing up whether it might be possible to go ahead with the privatisation without waiting for parliament to approve the regulatory authority.

As a result of the merger, the Treasury's stake in Stet will fall from 61.27 percent to 44.71 percent of ordinary shares. Prior to the merger, Stet owned some 63 percent of Telecom's ordinary stock and 20.9 percent of its savings shares.

Once the merger takes effect, Telecom Italia shareholders will receive one Stet ordinary share for every 1.8 Telecom ordinary shares and one Stet savings share for every 1.72 Telecom savings shares held.
The merger becomes operational on July 18 and shares in the new company, which will keep the name Telecom Italia, start trading on the following day.
Telecom shareholders voted in a new board of directors, to run the company in the lead-up to the merger, which is identical to the line-up on the Stet board.

Telecom Italia reported a 57 percent rise in 1996 net profits to 2.12 trillion lire ($1.7 billion), which was struck on turnover of 29.37 trillion lire. Stet's net profit last year was 1.11 trillion lire.

The government had originally set a target date of March 1997 for a sell-off to private investors but put it back late last year when it became clear parliament would be unable to pass laws needed to set up an independent regulatory agency.

Stet shareholders last month approved the introduction of a "golden share" giving the Treasury a power of veto for at least three years on key decisions such as acquisitions, asset disposals and choice of a core of stable shareholders.
The Treasury introduced a similar mechanism in energy group ENI's statutes before the sale of shares in the company to private investors in December 1995.

The privatisation of Stet is playing a key part in efforts by the government to reduce the debt mountain of Stet's former owner, state holding company IRI, to a level agreed with the European Union's executive Commission.
The government decided in November to transfer IRI's stake in Stet to the treasury and to pay IRI 14.53 trillion lire in return.
